body_text: How Multimodal Wearable Hardware Is Revolutionizing Human AI Interaction Artificial intelligence has driven software forward at an incredible rate over the past few years, but the hardware we use to interact with it has for the most part been stuck in the past. For more than twenty years, a small, glowing rectangle of glass in our pockets has served as the principal gateway to all digital information. Whether it’s to prompt a big language model, transcribe a quick voice note, summarize a meeting, or query a visual database, the process is always the same: grab a device, unlock it, open a specific app, and type out a command. This screen‑bounded model of interaction has a continuous physical friction. It forces us into a head‑down position, disrupting our real‑world focus and erecting an artificial wall between us and the people or places right in front of us. But there is a big shift underway in the wider tech ecosystem. With the ability of multimodal AI models to efficiently and quickly analyze real‑time visual streams and ambient audio, hardware engineers are finally embedding intelligence directly into the everyday accessories we already wear. Smart eyewear is at the forefront of this evolution, bringing digital tools out of the reactive screen of our smartphones and into hands‑free, ambient assistance right at eye level. The Rise of Multimodal Intelligence in Ambient Computing In traditional software interfaces, the user is always required to manually initiate the interaction. You need to open an app, type a prompt in a text box, or hold down a virtual button to talk into. That workflow works fine enough sitting at a desk with a laptop, but it falls apart completely when you are moving through the physical world, whether commuting through a crowded station, working on hands‑on technical projects, or traveling outdoors. Wearable AI glasses bridge this gap by putting optical sensors, directional open‑ear audio, and low‑power voice processing right on the human face. Embedding these components into a single wearable frame opens up a whole new suite of capabilities: Visual Question Answering: The optical camera is positioned directly in your natural line of sight, allowing the underlying AI to view what you see from a first‑person perspective. Rather than holding your phone up to take a picture, you can just ask questions out loud—tell me what this plant is while hiking, read foreign language street signs, or work your way through a physical assembly project step by step. Open‑Ear Audio Feedback: Tiny directional speaker arrays deliver crisp audio feedback directly to your temples. And unlike traditional earbuds, the speakers sit just outside of your ear canal, so you get 100% of your situational awareness. You can still be fully aware of ambient traffic, footsteps, and real‑time conversations while hearing incoming navigation cues or verbal summaries. Low‑Latency Voice Prompts: Today, spatial hardware does voice‑activity detection and lightweight machine learning tasks right on the physical device. This local processing greatly reduces transmission lag, so that digital interactions feel like an easy conversation with a companion, not a slow database lookup. As software developers continue to build out the underlying models that power ambient hardware, creators and tech‑minded professionals can explore the latest AI tools to discover specialized voice models, productivity platforms, and automated workflows that seamlessly fit into their daily routine. Where Lifestyle Design Meets High‑Performance Engineering Early smart glasses attempts didn’t catch on, as no one needs to be told. Older devices were heavy, ran uncomfortably hot, had short battery lives, and looked far too futuristic or industrial to be worn in public everyday. Who wants to be walking around with a bulky prototype on their face just to check their notifications? Happily, the initial design hurdles were overcome with modern hardware engineering, integrating micro‑components into lightweight, classic frames. Today’s consumers can have real personal style, best‑in‑class optical protection, and leading‑edge software features without compromise. Today’s consumers can have real personal style, best‑in‑class optical protection, and leading‑edge software features without compromise. Whether you pick up the best AI glasses from Sunglasshut or explore various smart frame styles online, you’ll find options that look and feel just like high‑end traditional sunglasses... That’s thanks to engineers who’ve carefully balanced the internal battery weight and micro‑circuits across the temple arms, eliminating the painful pressure points on the nose bridge that made heavy headsets so tiring to wear. This intelligent ergonomic compromise allows professionals, creators, and commuters to wear AI‑enabled glasses all day long without fatigue of the body or eyes. Edge Computing, Privacy, and Public Openness Of course, adding camera sensors and microphones to common glasses that people wear in public places raises important questions about user privacy, data security, and social etiquette. For wearable AI to gain the long‑term trust of the public, the core hardware architecture has to be completely transparent, protecting not only the wearer but those around them. To address these problems directly, leading hardware manufacturers are embedding compulsory safety and privacy protocols into the physical frame logic: Mandatory Privacy Indicators: Bright, high‑visibility LED indicator lights are hardwired directly to the camera power circuit. The LED will turn on brightly when a sensor is triggered or starts recording. It is hardware‑based so it cannot be disabled by software, providing an immediate and unmistakable notification to anyone in the area. On‑Device Cryptographic Encryption: Photos, video clips, and voice inputs are encrypted within the frame’s secure hardware element before anything syncs to cloud servers. This local isolation prevents data from being accessed without permission and protects personal notes from being intercepted over a network. Hardware Isolation: Users can totally power down the sensor modules using physical switches or simple gesture controls, ensuring ambient recording can never happen without the explicit awareness of the user. Digital rights groups such as the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) regularly note that strong user privacy controls, hardware isolation, and visible recording indicators are non‑negotiable standards for ensuring public trust as connected devices proliferate into shared spaces. The Next Frontier: Workflows Powered by AI As AI moves beyond the boundaries of web browser windows and into the physical world, screenless, face‑worn devices are poised to become the primary tool for how we capture, process, and organize our daily lives. Ambient hardware reduces the friction of the smartphone screen, so we can document spontaneous moments, navigate unfamiliar cities, and query intelligent models with our eyes up and our hands completely free. For creators, builders, and professionals looking to streamline their daily schedules, staying up to date with these hardware and software shifts is essential. You can discover new AI software solutions that will automate repetitive tasks, manage content pipelines, and build a more efficient, future‑ready digital toolkit. The future of technology is not about staring at a glowing screen in your palm—it is about moving through the physical world with complete focus, clarity, and intent. Tags tech industry

title: La Eurocopa Femenina 2025 hizo historia dentro y fuera del campo
summary: La Eurocopa Femenina de la UEFA 2025 ha sido uno de los grandes eventos deportivos del año, con una asistencia histórica de 657.291 espectadores a lo largo del torneo¹.
body_text: La Eurocopa Femenina de la UEFA 2025 ha sido uno de los grandes eventos deportivos del año, con una asistencia histórica de 657.291 espectadores a lo largo del torneo1. Antes de que el balón tocase el terreno de juego, en junio de 2025, ya observamos que el interés femenino por el fútbol en contenidos online creció un 25% en Reino Unido y un 17% en España, en comparación con el mismo periodo en 2022, año de la anterior Eurocopa 2. La gran final enfrentó a las Leonas de Inglaterra y a la Roja Femenina de España, dos selecciones que ofrecieron un juego sólido y emocionante durante todo el campeonato. El orgullo de sus aficiones se hizo notar en Basilea, ciudad anfitriona del encuentro, como vemos a continuación en estos vídeos de TikTok, publicados por la selección inglesa y el medio español Teledeporte. @england Bringing the noise in Basel #england #lionesses #weuro2025 #englandvsspain ♬ original sound - England @teledeportertve La Eurocopa empezó con ellos… ¡Y acaba de la misma forma! Las gaitas de ‘A Roda’ volvieron a sonar por las calles de Basilea para acompañar a los más de 3.000 aficionados españoles que van a disfrutar de la gran final de esta Eurocopa femenina 2025. Los tops de medios fueron BBC Sport con 321K total interacciones en un total de 41 posts y Teledeporte con 300K total interacciones en un total de 39 posts. Más allá del ámbito estrictamente deportivo, los medios de lifestyle, históricamente poco habituales en la cobertura futbolística, contribuyeron a la conversación digital de esta competición. Las redes sociales se hicieron eco de los momentos más emblemáticos, como la entrega del trofeo en Basilea y el dueto de la entrenadora Sarina Wiegman con su artista favorito, Burna Boy, en Londres. title: Under Armour and Bobby Witt Jr. Bring the Thrill of the “Perfect Pull” to the Diamond with the Dream Pull PE
summary: Bobby Witt Jr. and Under Armour introduce the Dream Pull PE, the shortstop’s first player-exclusive cleat. Inspired by Bobby’s deep passion for trading cards and the thrill of chasing a big hit, Dream Pull brings that energy to life by capturing the excitement of ripping packs and hunting for that perfect pull.
body_text: Built to translate the mindset of a collector into performance footwear, the footwear brings the feeling of a perfect pull to the diamond. On the side of the cleat and turf, the bubble features a lockup of Bobby Witt Jr.’s “JR” logo and the Under Armour logo printed inside. On the heel, the back bubble reads “GM,” referencing Gem Mint condition, while chromed, iridescent detailing creates a dynamic, light-shifting effect similar to a high-end parallel card. For the first time, fans can see, touch and wear Bobby’s “JR” logo and signature, embossed on the tongue of the Dream Pull cleat — a detail previously reserved for Bobby’s personal pairs.

title: Interactive Demo Platforms and Best Practices for 2026
summary: Guide into what interactive demos are, the different types of interactive demo software, and top-notch interactive demo examples.
body_text: Today, 18% of ~5,000 B2B SaaS websites have an interactive demo on their website, up 40% from last year, confirming growing buyer interest in self-guided evaluations. This stat is from our yearly State of the Interactive Product Demo . We used data from over 40,000 interactive demos built on Navattic to: Give benchmarks to compare your interactive demo metrics See what top-performing demos have in common Share best practices for demo format, length, and tone But with more and more companies adopting interactive demos, how can yours stand out? Below, we dive deeper into what interactive demos are, when to use them, and how to build outstanding demos that set your brand apart What is an interactive product demo? An interactive demo is a self-guided, clickable product walkthrough that lets prospects explore features at their own pace, without a live demo, sales rep, or trial setup. Interactive demos are a type of no-code sales demo software that gives prospects and customers a hands-on experience, without them ever having to log into your product. Though they aren't actually in your product (just in a replica of it), users still get a sense of what your product can do and whether it will serve their use case. What is the difference between interactive demos, demo automation, and agent demos These three terms get used interchangeably, but they mean different things: Interactive demo A self-guided, clickable walkthrough of your product that a prospect explores on their own Primary Use Cases: Website embeds, demo centers, email links Demo automation The broader practice of using interactive demos throughout the sales motion to remove manual steps from the buying process Primary Use Cases: Pre- and post-call leave-behinds, async follow-up, partner enablement Agent demo Agent demos interact with prospects, understanding their intent, and navigating your product and content in real time Primary Use Cases: Always-on website demos, qualifying inbound traffic without a rep Interactive demos and agent demos solve a similar problem (showing your product without a live rep) but work differently. An interactive demo is pre-built and the same for every visitor; an agent demo adapts based on what the visitor asks. That said, many interactive demo platforms, including Navattic, support a combination of all three. Letting teams run self-guided demos, automate demo workflows across the sales cycle, and deploy AI-powered agent demos from the same platform. Who uses interactive demos, and when? Because users don’t need access to your product to see it in action, you can use interactive demos across your entire funnel, from first-touch outbound emails to post-demo leave-behinds to upsell and cross-sell campaigns. Here's how different roles put interactive demos to work: Marketing teams embed demos directly on the website. Our data shows the most popular pages to place demos are product or solution pages (62%, up from 19% the year before), followed by the homepage (48%, up from 8%). Marketing also builds demo centers where prospects can explore multiple product tours on their own time. Sales reps use interactive demos as pre- or post-sales leave-behinds to accelerate discovery, personalize follow-ups, and shorten time to first call. Presales and solution engineers use sandbox demos to run live, hands-on walkthroughs on calls without the risk of bugs in a real environment. Partnerships teams use interactive demos for partner training , getting external sellers up to speed on product value props quickly. The best part? You don’t have to worry about users running into bugs, they’re in a fully controlled environment. How do I build an interactive demo? If you have the engineering resources, you could build interactive demos in-house. In most cases, though, using interactive demo software like Navattic is faster and doesn't require a dedicated engineering team. It can take six months to a year to build an interactive demo with dedicated engineers. In Navattic , anyone (sales, solution engineers, marketing, CS) can spin up a demo in a few hours, following five steps: Map out the user journey Capture product screens Use AI to speed up your build Tweak steps and text Optimize for mobile Below, we'll go into more detail on each one. Best practices for building a successful interactive demo 1. Map out user a-ha moments Great jumping-off points for demo content include: Sales calls Customer calls Webinars Frequently used slides One-pagers Load PDFs of those call recordings or your resources into your go-to LLM (like ChatGPT or Claude) and ask it to pull out two or three "a-ha moments" when users seemed particularly excited by your product. Run those a-ha moments by CS and Sales to confirm they're the right parts of the product to show. 2. Capture your product Most interactive demo tools will either be screenshots and videos or HTML/CSS-based. According to our research, 86% of top demos use web captures . HTML/CSS will make your product look and feel like the real thing by maintaining dynamic elements like hover states. As the marketing team at Phrase put it: "We did consider building a tour using screenshots and animations, but quickly realized that we were missing the 'in-product' feeling." HTML/CSS captures also let you edit the captures, meaning you can clean up messy demo data or personalize it to specific industries or prospects. To capture your product, you'll need to download a Chrome Extension from the interactive demo platform you choose. If you're using a product like Navattic, all you'll have to do is click through your product while using the Chrome extension, and our AI Copilot will generate a first draft of the demo for you. 3. Use AI to create a first draft Many demo tools can automatically build a first draft of a storyboard for you using AI. Navattic's AI Copilot , for example, automatically writes demo copy, anchor tooltips, and crafts a demo story based on your product context and best practices we've collected from the 40,000+ demos created on our platform. Once you have a first draft, you don't have to go back into the demo builder for every small fix. With Navattic's MCP , you can connect Navattic to Claude (or another LLM) and edit a demo's steps, copy, CTAs, and voiceover directly from a prompt, using whatever brand voice or style guide you already have set up in your LLM. When building your demo, here are best practices from our State of the Interactive Product Demo to keep in mind: Keep each demo flow between 5 to 13 steps. Flows with the highest completion rate run 1 to 6 steps. Incorporate two to four a-ha moments per demo. Use a modal as your first step. 72% of top demos start this way. Add visual beacons. 24% of top demos use them to guide attention to key areas. Address your users directly. 29% of top demos use "you/your" language. Create a theme that matches your company branding. Add a checklist to organize multiple flows and let users jump ahead. 4. Edit your demo Once you've got a draft demo in place, take some time to: Play with your colors. Black (28%) and white (17%) buttons are most common across top demos, as are dark, neutral dialogs over light or bright colors. Cut down your copy. The average word count is between 25 and 30 words per dialog box. Add internal CTAs. Top demos average 5 CTAs, typically concentrated in 1 to 2 steps. According to our research, more visitors move down-funnel with "Try for free" or "Book a demo" CTAs. Here are some more copywriting tips to boost conversion. Reposition your tooltips to see if you can offer a better UI. And if you'd like a second pair of eyes, reach out to us at support@navattic.com to schedule a demo review. After your demo has been live for a month or two, use Navattic's native drop-off reporting to see where people get stuck. Look at your demos with the highest engagement rates and see if you can apply some of the same techniques to your lower-performing ones. Not sure whether to gate your demo? This blog should help you make your decision. For what it's worth, our data shows 66% of top-performing demos are ungated, and ungated demos see roughly 6% higher engagement than gated ones. 5. Optimize your demo for mobile Just over half (52%) of top-performing demos have an optimized mobile experience. More buyers are doing vendor research on the go, and an unoptimized demo on mobile can kill a deal before it starts. Navattic offers three mobile options: Mobile Zoom: keeps your desktop layout intact with pinch-to-zoom. Best for complex demos or when demoing a mobile app. Mobile Swipe: a native swipe-right experience built for mobile-first audiences. Best for using demos in top-of-funnel campaigns. Mobile Alert: a fallback message or video for demos. As a general rule: if mobile is a primary channel for your audience (think social campaigns or event QR codes), use Mobile Swipe. If your desktop layout is essential to showing value, use Mobile Zoom. Read more about building mobile-friendly demos . Once your demo is ready, you can publish and share it live by adding it to your website or sending a link directly to prospects. 3 interactive demo examples To give you some inspiration, we’ve pulled several examples of how companies are using interactive demos on their websites. Lattice Use case: Navbar CTA, product pages Lattice, an AI-powered human resources software platform, uses click-through demos to show potential customers what the tool does and how it can drive performance, engagement, alignment, and compensation programs. On the homepage, users are invited to take a product tour in a CTA within the Platform section of the nav bar. The page reloads, and visitors are asked to provide some personal information. Once the form is filled out, Lattice customizes the tour experience based on whether the user is a manager or HR admin, ensuring they see what they will find most interesting and applicable to their day-to-day work. At the end of the demo, users can run through the alternate experience (Manager or HR Admin) — and Lattice tells them exactly what they’ll see — or book a call with the Lattice sales team. Explore Lattice’s Tour Vitally Type: Demo Center Vitally , an all-in-one customer success platform dedicates an entire section of its website to interactive demos: Building a library of various demos and adding filters for each core Vitally feature helps users find and walk through their exact use case. The demos are fairly in-depth, previewing to users just how much value they could get from the tool, thereby increasing the chances they convert. Explore the Vitally Academy Notion Type: Demo Center Notion, the all-in-one workspace for notes, docs, wikis, and project management, created a demo center to showcase its versatility across different teams and use cases. The demo center is organized by use cases, and each demo walks users through real-world scenarios, like how a marketing team might manage campaigns or how engineers can track sprints and documentation in one place. By organizing demos around team use cases rather than just features, Notion makes it easy for visitors to see the platform's value proposition for their specific needs. Watch a video walking through Notion's demos See more interactive demo examples on our customer showcase Top 7 interactive demo software plus pros and cons Picking the software you’ll use is just the first step in building an interactive demo. If you’re in the market for an interactive demo platform, here are some options to consider: Navattic for AI-powered interactive demos and agentic demos Storylane for early-stage startups who want to quickly build demos. Walnut for templated live sales demos to clone and personalize. Reprise for large, complex demo environments for live calls. Arcade for short how-to demos for social media or help articles. Tourial for Chrome extension-based apps or pre-live production apps. Supademo for small teams that want a cheap, easy-to-use demo platform To keep this article as unbiased as possible, we sourced pros and cons for each platform from the 3rd party sources G2 and Reddit. Navattic With Navattic, any team member can create HTML/CSS interactive or agentic demos that look and feel like your actual software without engineering help. Our product supports interactive demo builds for mobile apps, desktop apps, and other web-based tools. Our demo automation software lets sales reps send early-stage prospects async demos before and after live calls and save presales time from unqualified calls. Try an interactive demo of Navattic Our product integrates with tools in nearly every SaaS company’s tech stack and can connect to your AI tool of choice via our MCP. Pros Multi-purpose. Customers can use demos across their entire sales cycle. According to one customer, "I want to mention all the different ways I can use it to support our business, from sales enablement to internal education to conferences and now even POCs. I use it absolutely every day, and my work is essentially Navattic.” (G2 Review) No-code: Our product is all drag and drop, making it extremely easy to use. According to one of our customers, “The platform is incredibly easy to use and has thoughtful tools like allowing you to quickly edit out sensitive data and highlight certain components. It was a very low lift (less than a day!) to launch our first demo ( G2 Review ) AI Copilot: Create an entirely new demo just by clicking through your product. You can drop in custom prompts, and every demo it creates will reflect a specific demo use case with built-in demo best practices. Mobile view: Navattic has several viewing options for devices smaller than 800px wide, including smartphones and tablets. Cons Live demo options: Our focus on ease of use and fast deployments means we don’t specialize in overlays or click-anywhere demo sandboxes for live sales calls which can require a longer technical setup. Tour management complexity : Some users note challenges managing a growing number of interactive demos, especially when it comes to organizing versions and keeping content fresh ( G2 Review ). Pricing for 5 users Navattic’s Base plan is $100 per month per user. It comes with unlimited HTML demos, A/B testing, AI Copilot, Copilot Review, Copilot Prompt integrations, AI voiceovers and avatars, Narrated Demos, MCP access, and a dedicated CSM. Storylane With Storylane’s basic plan, users can create screenshot and video demos, directing users to specific features using text-based prompts. Storylane has some features to help build quick demos, like AI assist, which enriches voiceovers, translation, and copy. Storylane comes at a cheaper price, but it’s more of a self-serve tool — you don’t get a CSM isn't unless you go with their $1,200 minimum plan. Pros Demo Hub. Though Ignacio Harriague at Invgate didn’t end up going with Storylane, he shared: “Being able to build playlists or a gallery of demos so that prospects can pick and choose what they wanted to see was interesting. But we don’t sell too much into big enterprises where this would be useful.” Account reveal feature. “It’s loved by our sales team to see who is interacting with the demos on our website.” ( G2 Review ) Always visible CTA that can boost conversions “by keeping the call-to-action front and center.” ( Reddit ) Cons No HTML without a more expensive plan. Storylane customers don’t get a demo HTML editor, personalization, support, clickable live demos, or certain integrations unless they choose the $100 per user per month Growth plan. Lack of support. Nabilah Salleh at a customer communication platform went with Storylane but mentioned: “The help centers were lacking information.” Lack of analytics. Users say, “Would love to get clearer insights into which of our customers engage with the Tutorials we create,” and “The analytics part could be more intuitive for the administrator to make better calls on what to improve in the demo experience.” ( G2 Review , G2 Review ) Pricing for 5 users $500 per month. With the Growth plan, you get an HTML-guided demo, personalization (names, logos, dates, etc.), embedded lead forms, 10 integrations, 2,500 deanonymized visitors, and support. See our comparison landing page to learn more about Navattic vs Storylane. Walnut Walnut captures your product's front end with a Chrome extension and then allows users to edit and personalize through a no-code interface or HTML. Once a user finishes creating their demo, it’s added to a shared library, which can be categorized, saved for future use, or cloned and updated for a live call. A distinguishing characteristic of Walnut is that prospects can leave comments and questions as they go through a demo. AEs can respond asynchronously or use those comments as an entry point for another sales call. Pros Engagement. Prospects can leave comments and questions as they go through a demo, and AEs can respond asynchronously or use those comments as an entry point for another sales call. Shows off your integrations. If your product integrates with another software, you can capture both platforms and demo how they work together. “It helps showcase integrations with other platforms that often require SCs (clickthrough with a script they can follow). Has considerably cut down SC requests.” ( Reddit ) Cons Limited support for mobile apps. Walnut’s Chrome extension only works on web-based products. Users say, “Support for mobile apps is a little convoluted, but they seem to be working on it,” and “ We had some difficulty building Walnut demos from a mobile point of view because the platform only allows us to take screen captures from a web browser.” ( G2 Review , G2 Review ) Limited integrations. Walnut doesn’t have native integrations to Segment, Adobe Analytics, Mutiny, Amplitude, or Mixpanel. Getting up to speed takes time. “Other tools tend to have certain, what seems to be basic, functionality that Walnut lacks or requires customization. The building experience takes a bit longer to grasp, though a recent update has made it a bit easier.” ( G2 Review ) Pricing for 5 users Walnut charges a flat platform fee, though it’s unclear how many users are available in each of their three plans. Their Lite plan is $9,200 per year, with: Unlimited demos and website embeds Demo analytics HubSpot integration Walnut Uncover Playlists For a dedicated CSM, expert technical training, and integration with Salesforce, the platform fee skyrockets up to $20,000/year. Reprise In Reprise, users can build three kinds of demos: guided walk-throughs, live overlays, and cloned sandbox environments, so it makes sense for companies that need all three and want to centralize demo creation. That said, Reprise's complexity can steepen the learning curve for marketers, SEs, and AEs, and often requires engineering help. Like other sandbox demos, it opens you up to the same errors you could get in a live environment. Pros Supports large, complex demo environments for companies like Zendesk, MongoDB, and Databricks. Good customer service. “The customer and engineering support from Reprise has been helpful, and they have been able to accommodate specific use cases that required custom code.” ( G2 Review , G2 Review ) Cons Takes a while to get up to speed.
